label: L18
title: xHAIM: Improved Performance and Explainability
brief: Patients carry multimodal data (tabular, time series, images, notes), and the goal is to predict pathologies and outcomes from all of it. HAIM embeds each modality with a pretrained model, concatenates the embeddings and trains a final classifier, but it ingests too much irrelevant input, compresses everything into noisy embeddings and is a black box; a zero-shot LLM that reads everything as text cannot fit the input, is not trained on the data and gives poorly calibrated predictions. xHAIM converts modalities to text, retrieves the chunks most relevant to a task sentence (embedding similarity plus BM25), writes one compact summary per modality, fine-tunes ClinicalBERT on those summaries and feeds the resulting embeddings to the HAIM classifier. A generative model then combines the relevant chunks, summary, ML prediction and medical knowledge into an explanation that cites the raw patient records. On MIMIC-IV ICU data xHAIM raises ROC AUC over HAIM by up to about 20 points on pathology tasks and 2-3 points on mortality and length of stay, and LLM-as-a-judge scoring, validated against human annotators, rates its explanations on citation, factuality and quality across 1,000 cases.
kp: Multimodal patient data: tabular, time series, images, notes; tasks are pathologies (pneumonia) and outcomes (mortality, length of stay).
HAIM: modality-specific embeddings, concatenated (fusion), then a final classifier for any downstream task.
HAIM issues: too much often-irrelevant input, noisy single embedding, black box that hinders clinical adoption.
Zero-shot LLM issues: input too large, unsupervised and poorly calibrated, not trained on our data, hard to fine-tune proprietary LLMs on patient data.
xHAIM: define task keywords, retrieve relevant data, summarize, feed summaries into HAIM, generate grounded explanations.
Retrieval scores note chunks against a task sentence with embedding similarity (top-$k$) and BM25.
Short all-text summaries make fine-tuning ClinicalBERT on the dataset practical, giving tailored embeddings.
Explanations combine relevant chunks, summary, ML prediction and medical knowledge, with citations to raw text.
MIMIC-IV results (AUC %): pneumonia 76.3 to 96.7, pleural effusion 84.8 to 98.6, mortality 82.0 to 85.1; zero-shot LLM scores 44.7 on length of stay.
Explanation quality: rubric on citation, factuality, quality; LLM-as-a-judge validated on 100 human-annotated cases, then run on 1,000.

topics.n: The problem and the HAIM baseline
topics.x: Patients have tabular, time-series, image and note data, and the aim is to predict diagnoses or outcomes. HAIM turns each modality into an embedding with a modality-specific pretrained model, concatenates them and trains a final classifier, but the input is bloated and noisy and the model is a black box.

Convert every data source to text, hand it all to an LLM and ask for a prediction and explanation. The input is too large to fit, predictions are unsupervised and poorly calibrated, and the model is not trained on the hospital's data.

Step 0 defines the task and keywords; step 1 finds the most relevant patient data; step 2 writes one summary; step 3 feeds summaries into HAIM; step 4 explains. Modalities are converted to text (templates for tabular/time series, a multimodal LLM for images, notes as-is), notes are chunked, and chunks are scored against a task sentence with embedding similarity and BM25.

topics.n: Summaries, fine-tuning and the final classifier
topics.x: Each modality's top chunks become one compact paragraph. Because summaries are short and all text, ClinicalBERT can be fine-tuned on the dataset instead of relying on generic pretrained embeddings; the fine-tuned embeddings are concatenated and fed to the final classifier.

A generative model receives the relevant chunks, the generated summary, the ML prediction and medical knowledge, and writes an explanation that cites specific raw records, such as two radiology notes supporting a pleural-effusion prediction.

MIMIC-IV ICU data covered information-extraction tasks (pneumonia, pleural effusion, cardiomegaly) and prospective outcomes (48-hour mortality, ICU stay over 7 days). xHAIM beats HAIM and a zero-shot LLM on every task; the zero-shot LLM does well on extraction tasks but badly on outcomes.

A rubric scores citation quality, factual correctness and overall quality. Humans annotated 50 pleural-effusion and 50 mortality explanations; once a two-model LLM-as-a-judge (critic plus scorer) matched their score distributions, it scored 1,000 explanations. Mortality explanations score lower because evidence is hard to find even for humans.

cards.f: How does HAIM combine multimodal patient data?
cards.b: Each modality (tabular, time series, images, notes) is embedded by a modality-specific pretrained model; the embeddings are concatenated (fusion) and fed to a final classifier that can be trained for any downstream task.
cards.x: Fusion happens at the embedding level, not the raw-data level.

cards.b: (1) Too much input data, often irrelevant to the task. (2) Noisy classifier input, since one embedding must capture every detail. (3) No explainability (black box), which hinders adoption and clinical deployment.
cards.x: xHAIM attacks the first two with retrieval and summaries, the third with explanations.

cards.f: Zero-shot LLM approach and its four problems.
cards.b: Convert all sources to text, give the raw information to an LLM, ask for a prediction and explanation. Problems: too much input to fit; unsupervised predictions, not optimized for accuracy and poorly calibrated; not trained or fine-tuned on our data; fine-tuning proprietary LLMs on sensitive patient data is not trivial.
cards.x: Good explanations do not make good risk scores.

cards.b: 0: define task and keywords. 1: find the most relevant patient data. 2: produce one summary of all patient information. 3: feed summaries into HAIM for prediction. 4: combine ML predictions, summaries and raw data, and medical knowledge into GenAI explanations.
cards.x: Steps 1-3 improve input and predictions; step 4 adds transparency.

cards.f: How is each modality converted to text in xHAIM?
cards.b: Tabular and time series: natural-language templates (e.g. average and last blood pressure). Images with their reports: passed to a multimodal LLM (e.g. Qwen) that writes a description. Notes: used as-is.
cards.x: Tabular and time series can stay in regular HAIM, since xHAIM helps them less.

cards.f: How does xHAIM find the patient data relevant to a task?
cards.b: Define a task sentence of keywords (e.g. 'essential hypertension, hypertensive, high blood pressure, HTN, systolic, diastolic'), split notes into chunks, score each chunk by embedding similarity to the task sentence (keep top-$k$, e.g. 10) combined with BM25 keyword/frequency scoring, and keep the most relevant.
cards.x: Semantic plus lexical matching: synonyms via embeddings, exact terms via BM25.

cards.f: What is the per-modality summary and why use it?
cards.b: A uniform, comprehensive paragraph summarizing the patient's most relevant chunks for that modality. It is far more compact than the raw input, which can run to thousands of words.
cards.x: Dense, task-focused input replaces noisy raw data.

cards.f: Why can xHAIM fine-tune ClinicalBERT when HAIM used fixed pretrained embeddings?
cards.b: HAIM's embeddings (DenseNet for images, ClinicalBERT for notes) come from models trained on other data. xHAIM's summaries are short and every modality is text, so a pretrained text model like ClinicalBERT can be fine-tuned on the dataset for tailored representations.
cards.x: Text-izing everything makes one fine-tunable encoder possible.

cards.f: How is the final xHAIM prediction made, and why does it beat HAIM?
cards.b: Embeddings from the fine-tuned models are concatenated and fed to the final classifier, as in HAIM. Performance improves because the training data quality is much higher than the baseline's.

cards.f: Inputs and output of xHAIM's explanation step.
cards.b: Inputs: relevant chunks, generated summary, ML predictions, medical knowledge. Output: a GenAI explanation of the prediction with specific citations to the original raw text.
cards.x: Explains the ML model's prediction; does not replace it.

cards.b: MIMIC-IV ICU data (demographics, labs, chest X-rays, radiology and process reports). Information-extraction-like tasks: pneumonia, pleural effusion, cardiomegaly. Prospective outcomes: mortality within 48 hours, ICU length of stay over 7 days.
cards.x: Extraction tasks are stated in the notes; outcomes must be forecast.

cards.f: Pathology ROC AUC (%): HAIM vs zero-shot LLM vs xHAIM.
cards.x: Zero-shot LLM beats HAIM here, because the answer is written in the reports.

cards.f: Outcome ROC AUC (%): HAIM vs zero-shot LLM vs xHAIM.
cards.x: Zero-shot LLM falls below 50 on length of stay; gains from xHAIM are smaller (2-3 points) on outcomes.

cards.f: How were xHAIM explanations evaluated at scale?
cards.b: Rubric with three categories: citation quality, factual correctness, overall quality. Humans annotated 50 pleural-effusion and 50 mortality explanations. An LLM-as-a-judge (one model critiques, a second scores using critique and explanation) was trusted once its score distribution overlapped the humans', then scored 1,000 explanations.
cards.x: Validate the judge on human labels before scaling it.

cards.f: Why do mortality explanations score lower than pleural-effusion ones?
cards.b: For 'mortality within 48 hours' it is hard even for humans to find supporting evidence, such as citations, in the relevant documents.
cards.x: Explanation quality is bounded by how much evidence exists in the record.

quiz.q: In HAIM, how are the different data modalities combined for prediction?
o: Modality-specific embeddings are concatenated and fed to a final classifier
All data are converted to text and given to an LLM
One model per modality votes on the label
Images are captioned, and only the captions are used
quiz.e: HAIM fuses embeddings by concatenation, then trains a classifier. Converting everything to text and prompting an LLM is the zero-shot baseline.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT one of the HAIM weaknesses listed in the lecture?
o: It requires fine-tuning a proprietary LLM on sensitive patient data
It ingests too much data, often irrelevant to the task
Its classifier input is noisy because one embedding must capture every detail
It is a black box, which hinders clinical deployment
quiz.e: Fine-tuning proprietary LLMs on patient data is a zero-shot LLM problem. The other three are the HAIM issues on p.4.

quiz.q: Why are zero-shot LLM predictions a weak basis for clinical risk scores?
o: They are unsupervised, not optimized for accuracy, and poorly calibrated
LLMs cannot read radiology reports
They require labeled data at inference time
They only output binary labels
quiz.e: The LLM is never trained on the target, so its probabilities are not calibrated. It reads text well; the issue is supervision, not comprehension.

quiz.q: What is the correct order of the xHAIM steps?
o: Define task keywords, find relevant data, summarize, feed summaries into HAIM, generate explanation
Summarize all data, define task keywords, train HAIM, retrieve citations
Train HAIM on raw data, retrieve relevant chunks, summarize, explain
Generate explanation, then use it as a feature for HAIM
quiz.e: Steps 0-4 on p.7 run task definition, retrieval, summary, prediction, explanation. Summaries are built from retrieved chunks, so retrieval must come first.

quiz.q: Which xHAIM steps address 'too much data', and which address 'transparency'?
o: Retrieval and summarization address too much data; the GenAI explanation step addresses transparency
Fine-tuning ClinicalBERT addresses too much data; the classifier addresses transparency
The task sentence addresses transparency; the explanation addresses too much data
Both are solved by the final classifier
quiz.e: p.7 labels steps 1-2 as solving too much data and step 4 as solving transparency. Fine-tuning improves representations, not the volume of input.

quiz.q: How does xHAIM turn a chest X-ray into text?
o: The image and its report are given to a multimodal LLM (e.g. Qwen), which writes a description
A DenseNet embedding is decoded back into words
The image is dropped and only the radiology report is kept
Pixel statistics are written into a template sentence
quiz.e: Images go with their reports to a multimodal LLM. DenseNet embeddings belong to the original HAIM pipeline, not the text conversion.

quiz.q: Why might tabular and time-series data stay in the regular HAIM pipeline?
o: Applying xHAIM to them is less beneficial than to the other modalities
They cannot be expressed in natural language
BM25 cannot score numeric text
MIMIC-IV has no tabular data
quiz.e: The slide notes they can be templated into text but gain less from xHAIM. They clearly can be verbalized ('Patient is a 80 year old male').

quiz.q: How does xHAIM score note chunks for relevance to a task?
o: Embedding similarity to a task sentence (top-$k$) combined with BM25 keyword/frequency scoring
BM25 alone
Cosine similarity of the whole note to the label
Manual physician labeling of each chunk
quiz.e: Relevance combines semantic embedding similarity with lexical BM25. Using only one would miss either synonyms or exact clinical terms.

quiz.q: Four chunks score 0.95, 0.81, 0.67 and 0.87 against the task sentence. With top-$k$ retrieval and $k=2$, which are kept?
o: All four, since every score exceeds 0.5
quiz.e: Top-2 keeps the two highest scores, 0.95 and 0.87. Top-$k$ ranks; it does not apply a fixed threshold.

quiz.q: What makes fine-tuning ClinicalBERT practical in xHAIM?
o: Summaries are short and every modality is text, so one pretrained text model can be fine-tuned on the dataset
ClinicalBERT is already trained on MIMIC-IV, so no fine-tuning is needed
Images are fine-tuned with DenseNet instead
The zero-shot LLM supplies labels for fine-tuning
quiz.e: Short, all-text summaries let one text encoder be tailored to the data. The original HAIM used fixed pretrained embeddings trained on other data.

quiz.q: The final classifier architecture is the same in HAIM and xHAIM. What drives xHAIM's gain?
o: Higher-quality input: task-relevant summaries encoded by fine-tuned models instead of generic embeddings of raw data
A deeper final classifier
Using the LLM's prediction as an extra feature
Training on more patients
quiz.e: Embeddings are concatenated and classified as before; the gain comes from much better data quality. The slides do not add LLM predictions as features.

quiz.q: What does xHAIM's explanation generator take as input?
o: Relevant chunks, the generated summary, the ML prediction and medical knowledge
Only the ML prediction
The full raw EHR, unfiltered
Feature importances from the classifier
quiz.e: All four inputs are listed on p.14, so the explanation can cite raw text. Feature importances are not part of the pipeline.

quiz.q: Which task is a prospective outcome rather than an information-extraction-like task?
o: Mortality within 48 hours
Pneumonia
Pleural effusion
Cardiomegaly
quiz.e: Pathologies can be read off the reports; 48-hour mortality must be forecast.

quiz.q: From the results, what is xHAIM's absolute ROC AUC gain over HAIM for pneumonia?
o: 20.4 points
6.8 points
13.8 points
2.2 points
quiz.e: 96.7 - 76.3 = 20.4. 6.8 is the gain over the zero-shot LLM (89.9), 13.8 is the pleural-effusion gain over HAIM, 2.2 the length-of-stay gain.

quiz.q: The zero-shot LLM scores 44.7% ROC AUC on length of stay. How should this be read?
o: Worse than random ranking: zero-shot reasoning fails on a prospective outcome it was never trained to predict
Strong performance, since AUC above 40 is good
Evidence that length of stay is unpredictable for any model
A calibration issue that would vanish after thresholding
quiz.e: AUC below 50 ranks patients worse than chance. HAIM (75.5) and xHAIM (77.7) predict it well, so the task is learnable; AUC is threshold-free, so thresholding cannot fix it.

quiz.q: Why was LLM-as-a-judge compared with human annotators before scoring 1,000 explanations?
o: To confirm its score distribution overlaps the humans' before trusting it at scale
To train the judge on the human labels
Because humans scored all 1,000 cases anyway
To pick which LLM generates the explanations
quiz.e: Humans scored 100 explanations; adequate overlap justified using the judge for 1,000. The judge is validated, not trained, on them.

quiz.q: Why do mortality explanations score lower than pleural-effusion ones?
o: Evidence for 48-hour mortality is hard to find in the documents, even for humans
The mortality classifier has a lower AUC than any other task
The judge was not validated on mortality cases
Mortality explanations were not given citations
quiz.e: The slide attributes it to scarce citable evidence. The judge was validated on 50 mortality cases, and mortality AUC (85.1) is not the lowest (length of stay is 77.7).

quiz.q: The zero-shot LLM beats HAIM on all three pathologies but loses on both outcomes. Which explanation fits the lecture?
o: Pathologies are stated in the reports, so reading suffices; outcomes need a model trained on our data, which zero-shot lacks
LLMs are better with images than with notes
HAIM was not trained on pathology labels
Outcomes have more missing data, which LLMs cannot handle
quiz.e: Extraction-like tasks reward reading comprehension, while prospective outcomes need supervised learning and calibration, the gaps listed on p.6. The other options are not supported by the slides.

written.q: A hospital wants to predict hypertension from ICU records (structured data, chest X-rays with reports, clinical notes) and show clinicians why. (a) Describe the xHAIM pipeline end to end for this task, including how each modality becomes model input. (b) For each step, state which weakness of HAIM or of a zero-shot LLM it addresses.
written.m: (a) Step 0: define the task and a task sentence of keywords, e.g. 'essential hypertension, hypertensive, high blood pressure, HTN, systolic, diastolic'. Convert modalities to text: structured and time-series data via templates (or keep them in regular HAIM, where xHAIM helps less), X-rays plus reports via a multimodal LLM such as Qwen, notes as-is. Step 1: split notes into chunks and score them against the task sentence with embedding similarity (top-$k$, e.g. 10) and BM25; keep the most relevant. Step 2: write one compact summary paragraph per modality from those chunks. Step 3: fine-tune ClinicalBERT on the summaries, concatenate the resulting embeddings and train the final HAIM classifier. Step 4: a GenAI model combines the relevant chunks, summary, ML prediction and medical knowledge into an explanation citing the raw records. (b) Retrieval and summaries fix HAIM's irrelevant, bloated input and the LLM's context limit; fine-tuned embeddings of dense summaries fix HAIM's noisy generic embeddings; keeping a supervised classifier fixes the zero-shot LLM's lack of training and calibration and avoids fine-tuning a proprietary LLM on patient data; the grounded explanation fixes HAIM's black-box problem.
k: Modality-to-text conversion, including multimodal LLM for images
Chunking plus embedding similarity and BM25
Fine-tuned ClinicalBERT feeding the HAIM classifier
Each step mapped to a named weakness

written.q: Using the lecture's results: (a) compare HAIM, the zero-shot LLM and xHAIM on pathology versus outcome tasks, with numbers, and explain the pattern. (b) Describe how explanation quality was measured and why the LLM judge could be trusted. (c) Why are mortality explanations harder to produce?
written.m: (a) Pathologies (AUC %): pneumonia 76.3 / 89.9 / 96.7, pleural effusion 84.8 / 93.7 / 98.6, cardiomegaly 81.1 / 91.1 / 98.2. Outcomes: length of stay 75.5 / 44.7 / 77.7, mortality 82.0 / 78.5 / 85.1. The zero-shot LLM beats HAIM where the answer is written in the reports but fails on prospective outcomes (below chance on length of stay) because it is unsupervised and not trained on the data. xHAIM wins everywhere: about 14-20 points over HAIM on pathologies and 2-3 points on outcomes, matching the 'up to 2-20%' claim. (b) A rubric scores citation quality, factual correctness and overall quality. Humans annotated 50 pleural-effusion and 50 mortality explanations; an LLM-as-a-judge (one model critiques, another scores using the critique) was run on the same cases, and adequate overlap of score distributions justified using it on 1,000 explanations. (c) For mortality within 48 hours the documents rarely contain direct evidence, so even humans struggle to find citations, and citation and factuality scores fall.
k: Correct numbers for both task groups
Extraction vs prospective explanation of the LLM pattern
xHAIM gain size on each group
Human validation before scaling the judge
Scarce evidence explains weaker mortality explanations
